rendered:
The paper gives no amount (no concentration or mass) for nickel, manganese or cobalt leaching into Cyrene. It reports that they did not leach: the relative ratios of Ni, Mn and Co in NMC622 were consistent before and after separation, which the authors say shows the process [1]. The ICP-OES confirmation is given in in Table S1[2], a supplementary table that is not included in this document, so no ICP-OES numbers are available here.

The only leaching the paper describes is of lithium, which it says occurred after recovery. The stated reason is the solvent's chemistry. The Cyrene molecule has two ether groups,[3] which will attract lithium cation because ether is electron-donating,[4] resulting in lithium leaching and causing the high-Ni cathode more[5] unstable. In the authors' account, the ether groups pull lithium out of the cathode, which makes the high-nickel cathode less stable, while nickel, manganese and cobalt stayed in the material.
